bp: A short-video advertising platform has to decide, for each user and advertiser, how likely an ad click is to turn into a real purchase or other conversion. On ordinary days, yesterday's behavior is often a useful teacher: people browse, click, and buy in roughly familiar rhythms. Large shopping promotions break that rhythm. Around Black Friday or 618 Shopping Day, users wait for discounts, advertisers change bids and campaigns, traffic composition changes, and the meaning of a click can shift sharply. TemporalExpertNet serves this practical moment. It is trying to keep conversion-rate prediction useful when the platform enters a known but unusual season. The paper treats promotion periods not as random noise, but as recurring temporal regimes with reusable knowledge. Its goal is to reuse what was learned from earlier promotion cycles while still adapting to the current users, advertisers, and features on a large short-video ads platform.
wh: The hard part is that promotion behavior changes in uneven ways. Some patterns stay stable: a user's broad interests, an advertiser's product category, and general ad-response clues may still matter. Other patterns become promotion-sensitive: users may delay buying until the sale, advertisers may push different creatives, and the same feature value can mean something different during preheating than during a normal day. A single daily model tends to mix these two kinds of evidence into one set of learned habits. If it trusts normal-day patterns too much, it underreacts to the sale. If it overfits one old promotion, it may reuse stale behavior when the current promotion has different shoppers or advertisers. The abstract also says the shifts are heterogeneous, which means not every sample needs the same adjustment. The model therefore needs both temporal reuse and sample-level caution: borrow the right historical knowledge, align it with current features, and decide case by case how much of it to use.
naive: A smart beginner might train a strong conversion model on daily data, then keep using it through the promotion. That fails because the training examples mostly describe ordinary behavior, while the sale period changes both user intent and advertiser strategy. Another beginner fix is to train a separate model for each promotion period. That can capture sale-specific behavior, but it wastes repeated structure across promotions and may be weak when the current promotion has limited fresh labels. A third fix is to fine-tune the old model on current data. The abstract suggests this is still too rigid because historical knowledge and current features may not line up cleanly, and different samples need different mixes of stable and promotion-sensitive knowledge.
ap: TemporalExpertNet's central move is to split the predictor into parts with different jobs. One part is a stable representation encoder: it tries to preserve the recurring signals that remain useful across time, such as broad user, ad, and context patterns. Another part is a promotion-sensitive expert: it focuses on the behavior that changes during promotion cycles. The paper then adds two bridges between past and present. BridgeNet handles the mismatch between historical temporal knowledge and current features by aligning their internal descriptions, so old promotion knowledge is not pasted onto the present in the wrong coordinate system. TemporalExpertGate performs sample-aware expert fusion, meaning it chooses, for each example, how much to trust different expert knowledge. The method is therefore not simply a bigger predictor. It is a controlled reuse machine: keep stable signals, adapt sale-sensitive signals, and gate their mixture according to the current sample.
mech: The mechanism starts with logged advertising examples from ordinary days and promotion periods. Each example contains current features about a user, advertiser, ad situation, and later conversion outcome. First, the stable encoder turns the raw features into a compact description meant to carry patterns that should survive across time. This is the part the system wants to reuse rather than relearn from scratch for every sale. Next, the promotion-sensitive expert models the part of the prediction that changes when a promotion cycle alters browsing and buying behavior. Historical promotion knowledge cannot simply be copied, because feature meanings and population mix can change. BridgeNet therefore aligns the historical temporal description with the current feature description, reducing the mismatch between what the old promotion expert knows and what the present sample looks like. Then TemporalExpertGate reads the sample and decides how to fuse expert outputs. For one user-ad pair, the stable encoder may be enough; for another, a sale-specific expert may deserve more weight. Training happens in two stages, according to the abstract: first to make alignment stable, then to learn adaptive expert fusion. The output is a conversion-rate score used by the ads platform to rank or allocate impressions during the 618 preheating phase.
math: The mathematical ideas are learning from examples, temporal transfer, alignment, weighted expert mixing, and error reduction. Learning from examples means the system sees many past cases where features were followed by conversion or no conversion, then learns a scoring rule that gives higher scores to cases that looked like later converters. Temporal transfer means reusing patterns from an earlier time period because the current period has a related shape. The danger is false reuse: yesterday's sale knowledge may be close enough to help, or different enough to hurt. Alignment is the mathematical repair for that danger. It changes internal descriptions from historical and current data so comparable cases are brought into a shared language before they are reused. Expert mixing means several specialized predictors produce advice, and a gate assigns weights to their advice for each sample. A weight is a controlled amount of trust, not a permanent rule. The two-stage training is an error-reduction process: define what counts as a bad alignment or bad conversion prediction, then adjust model settings to reduce that badness. The tradeoff is stability versus adaptability. Keep too much stable knowledge and the sale shift is missed; trust the promotion expert too much and current predictions may chase short-lived noise.
dots: This paper sits where recommendation, advertising, ranking, and time-aware prediction meet. Like other conversion-rate papers in the repo, such as ChorusCVR and discount-aware CVR modeling, it asks why a click or ad impression should be trusted as evidence of later buying. Its special pressure is time: the same marketplace behaves differently during promotion cycles. That connects it to the time-series family, where the recurring lesson is that past structure helps only after the system separates stable rhythm from sudden change. It also connects to mixture-of-experts ideas in commerce, such as delayed GMV prediction with routing, because both split cases that should not be averaged into one predictor. At the platform level, the predicted conversion rate becomes part of ranking and ad allocation: which ad deserves scarce exposure now? TemporalExpertNet's answer is that ranking during a sale should not be driven by a flat daily model, but by a temporally adjusted score that knows when old promotion knowledge is relevant.
ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it matches the actual shape of promotion data. Promotions are not completely new worlds, so throwing away old knowledge is wasteful. They are also not ordinary days, so treating all history as equally current is misleading. By separating a stable encoder from a promotion-sensitive expert, the model gives each kind of evidence a proper place. BridgeNet helps because reuse only works when the thing being reused is compared in the same internal language as the current sample. If historical promotion patterns and present features are misaligned, the model may apply a past rule to the wrong kind of user or advertiser. The gate helps because heterogeneous shifts mean no single adjustment is right for everyone. A bargain hunter in a sale category may need strong promotion-specific correction, while another user-ad pair may still follow ordinary behavior. Sample-aware fusion lets the model vary that trust continuously. The reported small model-size and latency overhead also matter: the mechanism is useful only if it can run inside an industrial ads system without slowing serving too much.
po: The payoff is a promotion-aware conversion predictor that can be deployed rather than only studied offline. The abstract reports that TemporalExpertNet was used on a large short-video ads platform during the 618 preheating phase. It improved conversion rate by 7.52 percent and platform revenue per mille by 4.27 percent, while adding only 0.23 percent model size and 1.8 percent latency overhead. In practical terms, the system buys better sale-period ad ranking with modest serving cost. It lets the platform reuse past promotion knowledge without assuming every promotion, user, and advertiser behaves identically.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. Past promotion cycles must contain knowledge that is genuinely reusable for the current cycle; if the current sale has different products, policies, users, discounts, or advertiser tactics, transfer can mislead. BridgeNet assumes historical and current descriptions can be aligned well enough for reuse. The gate assumes the model has enough evidence to decide which expert to trust for each sample. The abstract reports deployment during one 618 preheating phase on a short-video ads platform, but it does not prove the same gains for other platforms, sale types, countries, or longer post-sale periods. It also reports business metrics, not detailed failure analysis for minority advertisers, cold-start campaigns, or adversarial promotion behavior.
